guidelineTitle: Guías prácticas de diagnóstico y tratamiento del síndrome de apneas e hipopneas obstructivas del sueño: Actualización 2018
recommendation: "La aplicación de presión positiva continua en la vía aérea (CPAP) durante el sueño es el tratamiento de elección para el SAHOS" (CPAP is the treatment of choice) (Recomendación A). Indicated for AHI >= 15/h, or AHI 5-14.9 with daytime sleepiness, cognitive deficit, or cardiovascular/metabolic/cerebrovascular disease (A). "La indicación, ajuste y control del tratamiento debe estar a cargo de un equipo profesional entrenado en Medicina del Sueño" (sleep-medicine team prescribes and follows). Auto-CPAP titration at home allowed (A).

guidelineTitle: Guías prácticas de diagnóstico y tratamiento del síndrome de apneas e hipopneas obstructivas del sueño: Actualización 2018
recommendation: "La evidencia disponible muestra que la PR realizada en el domicilio del paciente es comparable a la PSG realizada en el laboratorio de sueño para el diagnóstico del SAHOS del adulto en pacientes con sospecha clínica. (Evidencia A)" (home respiratory polygraphy is comparable to lab PSG in adults with clinical suspicion). Expert reading needed with heart/lung disease, neuromuscular disease, stroke, chronic opioids. Valid study needs >= 4 h interpretable recording.

body: Australasian Sleep Association + Sleep Health Foundation + RACGP + Australian Psychological Society + Pharmaceutical Society of Australia + APNA (joint position statement)
guidelineTitle: Management of adult insomnia in Australia (joint position statement)
recommendation: "Multi-component Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for insomnia (CBTi) is the recommended 'first-line' treatment for insomnia", effective across settings, comorbidities and modes (individual, group, telehealth, self-guided digital). Sleep hygiene advice "not an adequate stand-alone treatment for chronic insomnia". "Clinicians should discuss CBTi options with all patients with insomnia as the first-line management approach."
conflictsOfInterest: Funded by Australian Government Health Peak and Advisory Bodies grant (2022-2026) and a Quality Use of Diagnostics, Therapeutics and Pathology grant. Disclosures: lead author was salaried ASA staff; one author (DC) made GP podcast content sponsored by Eisai (lemborexant maker); one author owns a behavioural sleep clinic.

body: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP)
guidelineTitle: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice, Part B: Benzodiazepines
status: stale (published 2015; page notes may not reflect current evidence)
recommendation: "First-line therapy should be non-drug interventions" and CBT "should therefore be offered to patients, including older adults" (Level A). "Short-term or intermittent dosing of benzodiazepines should be used to reduce the risk of tolerance and dependence" (Level B). "Long-term use, beyond 4 weeks, should be uncommon". Stepped approach to discontinuation.
strength: Level A (non-drug first line); Level B (short/intermittent)

recommendation: Free CPAP loan for Queensland residents holding a Pensioner Concession Card, Health Care Card or DVA white card, with "significant sleep apnoea" diagnosed at a QHSDP Prescriber Centre, managed by an RACP-accredited sleep physician; must first rent a device for a "minimum 2-month home treatment trial with average usage of at least 4 hours per night"; buy own mask. Access needs GP or specialist referral.

guidelineTitle: MBS items 12203 (attended PSG) and 12250 (unattended home study)
recommendation: Item 12250 (home study, adults 18+) is payable if either (i) a medical practitioner (e.g. GP) refers to a sleep or respiratory physician who determines high probability of symptomatic moderate-severe OSA "based on a STOP-Bang score of 3 or more, an OSA50 score of 5 or more or a high risk score on the Berlin Questionnaire, and an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score of 8 or more"; or (ii) the specialist sees the patient (face-to-face or video) and decides a test is needed. Item 12203 (lab PSG) has the same gate plus listed indications (e.g. not suitable for home study, central apnoea, hypoventilation).

guidelineTitle: MBS item 12204 (CPAP titration study)
recommendation: Attended PAP titration study payable when need is decided by a qualified adult sleep medicine practitioner or respiratory physician, who has seen the patient (face-to-face or video) and established the breathing disorder causes the symptoms; patient has not had PAP in the previous 6 months. Medicare does not subsidise the CPAP device itself.

guidelineTitle: AusPAR: Slenyto (melatonin)
status: current; a 2026 AusPAR reportedly extends the indication
recommendation: The 2020 approval covers insomnia in ages 2-18 with ASD and/or Smith-Magenis syndrome, where sleep hygiene is insufficient. Starting dose is 2 mg, maximum 10 mg. Prescription only. A TGA decision of 15 May 2026 reportedly extends this to neurogenetic disorders and adds ADHD for ages 6-17.

body: Associação Brasileira do Sono (ABS) + Associação Brasileira de Medicina do Sono (ABMS)

body: Sociedade Brasileira de Pneumologia e Tisiologia (SBPT)
guidelineTitle: Brazilian Thoracic Association Consensus on Sleep-disordered Breathing
recommendation: "Positive pressure therapy is the treatment of choice for individuals with moderate-to-severe OSA." Adherence defined as CPAP >= 4 h/night on >= 70% of nights in the first 3 months. Other options: positional therapy, alcohol avoidance, exercise, weight loss, oral appliances, surgery.

body: Sociedade Brasileira de Pneumologia e Tisiologia (SBPT)
guidelineTitle: Brazilian Thoracic Association Consensus on Sleep-disordered Breathing
recommendation: High-risk patients (by screening) "can be tested either at home or in the sleep laboratory"; low-risk should be tested in the lab. A negative or technically poor home study with high suspicion should be followed by in-lab PSG. Screening tools can route high-risk patients to home testing "thus trimming the waiting lists at sleep laboratories."

body: Choosing Wisely Canada / Canadian Geriatrics Society
guidelineTitle: Geriatrics: Recommendation 2
recommendation: "Don't use benzodiazepines or other sedative-hypnotics in older adults as first choice for insomnia, agitation or delirium." Supporting text: number needed to treat for better sleep is 13, number needed to harm is 6; CBT and taper protocols help discontinuation.

guidelineTitle: Management of Chronic Insomnia
recommendation: Taper BZRAs by "no more than diazepam 5mg or clonazepam 0.25mg equivalent per week" (slower below 20 mg diazepam-equivalent), or reduce 10% every 1-2 weeks until 20% remains, then 5% every 2-4 weeks; follow up every 1-4 weeks; consider CBT.

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia disorder (2025 edition) 失眠症诊断和治疗指南（2025版）
recommendation: CBT-I is stressed and recommended as the first-line treatment for insomnia. Its five core parts are sleep hygiene, stimulus control, sleep restriction, relaxation and cognitive therapy. It can be given one-to-one (weekly, 30-60 min, 4-8 sessions), in groups of 5-8, or digitally. New additions: mindfulness, circadian support and intensive sleep retraining.

recommendation: To switch drugs, lower the old one step by step while starting and raising the new one. To cut down, reduce the bedtime dose gradually or move to intermittent use. Avoid stopping suddenly; tapering can take weeks to months. In older adults use fewer drugs, start low and keep courses short.

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia disorder (2025 edition)
recommendation: Drugs should not be the first choice. Use them on top of treating the cause, CBT-I and sleep health education, following the principles 'individualised, as needed, intermittent, adequate dose, short course' (个体化、按需、间断、足量、短疗程). Recommended order: first, orexin antagonists (DORA) together with short- and intermediate-acting benzodiazepine receptor agonists (BZRA); second, other BZRAs or melatonin receptor agonists (ramelteon, tasimelteon, agomelatine); third, sedating antidepressants (only doxepin, mirtazapine and trazodone, with fluvoxamine dropped from the 2017 list). Quetiapine and olanzapine are not recommended for general insomnia, and nor is gabapentin.

recommendation: Has a full traditional Chinese medicine section. Insomnia is treated as 'bu mei' (不寐病) by pattern differentiation (辨证论治), mainly following the National Administration of TCM standard. A table pairs each pattern with herbal formulas, e.g. liver-qi stagnation → Chaihu Shugan San or Xiaoyao San. Combined care is encouraged: CBT-I plus drugs, physical therapy or TCM, or drugs plus TCM or physical therapy.

recommendation: PAP is recommended first-line for moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI ≥15/h) (1A). It may be considered for mild OSA with cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, COPD or marked symptoms, and around surgery (1B). Fixed CPAP is the default because it costs less (1A). Auto-PAP is for people who cannot tolerate CPAP or have positional or variable OSA. Pressure titration is recommended before starting; full-night in-lab titration is the gold standard, and split-night or home auto-titration are acceptable for moderate-to-severe OSA (1A).

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in adults (2025)
recommendation: Drugs are not routine treatment for OSA (1A). For moderate-to-severe OSA with obesity not controlled by diet and exercise, tirzepatide may be considered as an add-on (1A). For daytime sleepiness that remains despite good OSA treatment, solriamfetol or modafinil is recommended (1A). For sleepiness in people who refuse or cannot use standard treatment, solriamfetol is recommended (1A) and modafinil may be considered (2B). For OSA with insomnia (COMISA), short-term non-benzodiazepine hypnotics may be considered under close monitoring or with CPAP (1B); benzodiazepines are not recommended (1A).
strength: 1A (tirzepatide; solriamfetol/modafinil residual EDS); 1A against benzodiazepines in COMISA

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in adults (2025)
recommendation: In-lab polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard (1A) and comes first for complex cases and high-risk jobs. Home testing (HSAT) is recommended for suspected moderate-to-severe uncomplicated OSA, but not for screening people without symptoms or for diagnosing mild OSA (1A). Diagnose with ICSD-3-TR criteria and grade severity mainly by AHI.

guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in adults (2025)
recommendation: Oral appliances are recommended for primary snoring and mild-to-moderate OSA, and as an alternative or add-on for people who cannot tolerate or keep using PAP (1A). Custom-made devices are preferred. Mouth and throat muscle exercises (myofunctional therapy) are recommended as an add-on (1A). Upper-airway surgery may be considered for clear anatomical problems in people who cannot use PAP (1A).

body: Chinese Thoracic Society (CMA), Sleep Disordered Breathing Assembly
guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in adults (2025)
recommendation: Routine screening of the general population is not recommended (1A). Screen high-risk people with symptoms, signs or related conditions, plus surgical candidates and drivers or workers in safety-critical jobs (1A). Use STOP-Bang (1A); Berlin or STOP may also be used (1B). ESS measures sleepiness but must not be used to diagnose. Questionnaires alone must not diagnose OSA (1A). Validated consumer wearables can help people screen themselves but must not replace medical-grade testing (1A). In resource-limited primary care, simplified criteria using history, examination and pulse oximetry may be used (1A).

body: Expert consensus (Rome conference 2014; European paediatric neurologists)
guidelineTitle: Current role of melatonin in pediatric neurology: clinical recommendations
recommendation: 'The best evidence for efficacy is in sleep onset insomnia and delayed sleep phase syndrome. It is most effective when administered 3-5 h before physiological dim light melatonin onset. There is no evidence that extended-release melatonin confers advantage over immediate release.' Children with ASD, ADHD and intellectual disability 'can benefit'. Melatonin shortens time to fall asleep and increases total sleep 'but does not decrease night awakenings'.

They may be advised not to drive until confirmation of the diagnosis.' 11.4: licences may be issued if 'adequate control of their condition and compliance with appropriate treatment and improvement of sleepiness'. 11.5: periodic review 'at intervals not exceeding three years for drivers of group 1 and one year for drivers of group 2'.

recommendation: 'la durée maximale de prescription est limitée à 12 semaines pour les anxiolytiques et 4 semaines pour les hypnotiques'. Prescribing 'ne doit être envisagée qu'après échec des approches non médicamenteuses' and 'ne doit pas dépasser les durées préconisées dans l'AMM'.

guidelineTitle: Avis relatif aux risques liés à la consommation de compléments alimentaires contenant de la mélatonine (saisine n° 2016-SA-0209)
status: current opinion (2018); regulatory status may have changed
recommendation: In France melatonin is on list II of 'substances vénéneuses' (since 2011); Circadin 2 mg PR is a prescription medicine for primary insomnia ≥55 y. 'Actuellement les compléments alimentaires contenant moins de 2 mg de mélatonine par prise sont autorisés par décision administrative de la DGCCRF'. ANSES lists at-risk groups (pregnant/breastfeeding, children/adolescents, autoimmune disease, epilepsy, asthma, mood disorders, people needing sustained vigilance) and says not to combine with medicines without a doctor's advice.

body: Ministère de la Santé (arrêté du 7 janvier 2017), reported by VIDAL
guidelineTitle: Zolpidem: prescription sur ordonnance sécurisée
status: current (from 10 April 2017; verify no later change)
recommendation: From 10 April 2017 zolpidem must be prescribed on an 'ordonnance sécurisée' (secure prescription form), with number of units, doses and strength written 'en toutes lettres'; overlapping prescriptions forbidden unless stated; prescription remains 'limitée à 28 jours'.

body: Société de Pneumologie de Langue Française (SPLF) with 6 other societies
guidelineTitle: Recommandations pour la pratique clinique du syndrome d'apnées hypopnées obstructives du sommeil de l'adulte
status: stale (2010); HAS notes a re-evaluation of recommendations is under way
recommendation: Content not read (only PubMed record, no abstract). Listed to record that France's clinical OSA guideline dates from 2010.

body: Haute Autorité de Santé - CNEDiMTS (payer listing, LPPR)
guidelineTitle: Dispositifs médicaux de pression positive continue (PPC) et prestations associées dans la prise en charge du SAHOS - Partie 2: Révision des conditions de prise en charge (avis adopté 3 mars 2026)
recommendation: Initial prescription and renewal by a pneumologist, or a physician with a sleep FST/DES training (proposed minimum 40 h specific to sleep breathing disorders), or a validated sleep DPC pathway, or a recognised sleep diploma. Initial prescription valid 4 months; renewal yearly. From the third prescription, renewal may be done by the GP ('médecin traitant') or a trained nurse under a cooperation protocol if the patient shares adherence data meeting the 10-of-12 rule. PG/PSG must be done by a physician; the CPAP provider may not take part in diagnosis.

body: Haute Autorité de Santé - CNEDiMTS (payer listing, LPPR)
guidelineTitle: Dispositifs médicaux de pression positive continue (PPC) et prestations associées dans la prise en charge du SAHOS - Partie 2: Révision des conditions de prise en charge (avis adopté 3 mars 2026)
status: current listing criteria; HAS proposals (March 2026) not yet in force by arrêté as far as found
recommendation: Adults (>16 y) need ≥3 of: daytime sleepiness, severe daily snoring, choking/suffocation in sleep, daytime fatigue, nocturia, morning headache; PLUS AHI ≥30/h (polygraphy or PSG), OR AHI 15-29/h on PSG with severe sleepiness and/or accident risk, OR AHI 15-29/h with serious cardiovascular or respiratory comorbidity. 'En première intention, le prescripteur doit, avant d'effectuer toute prescription d'une prestation de PPC, examiner l'alternative ... d'une prescription d'orthèse d'avancée mandibulaire' if criteria met. Prior authorisation (accord préalable) with the PG/PSG report is required. Auto-CPAP or fixed CPAP first; bilevel only after failure.

body: Haute Autorité de Santé - CNEDiMTS (payer listing, LPPR)
guidelineTitle: Dispositifs médicaux de pression positive continue (PPC) et prestations associées dans la prise en charge du SAHOS - Partie 2: Révision des conditions de prise en charge (avis adopté 3 mars 2026)
status: current rule; proposed stop rule pending
recommendation: Adherence measured per 28-day period: patient 'doit utiliser effectivement son dispositif médical de PPC pendant au moins 112 heures'; 56-111 h tolerated temporarily; '<56 heures par période de 28 jours doit être considérée comme médiocre'. Counting starts week 14 of treatment. Annual renewal without prior authorisation if ≥112 h in at least 10 of the last 12 periods and ≥56 h in the other two. Provider must alert prescriber if <112 h. Weekly provider fee is tiered by usage. HAS (3 March 2026) also proposes that after a maximum of 3 months of support, stopping can be considered if use stays <56 h per 28 days.

body: French Society of Sleep Research and Medicine (SFRMS) expert group
guidelineTitle: Management of obstructive sleep apnea syndrome type 1 in children and adolescents - A French consensus
recommendation: 'A specialist otolaryngologist examination, including nasofibroscopy, is essential during diagnosis. A sleep study for OSA1 is not mandatory when at least two nighttime symptoms (including snoring) are noted.' ENT surgery is often required, and orthodontic treatment with orofacial myofunctional therapy may be indicated. Follow-up is multidisciplinary.
conflictsOfInterest: Several authors report speaker or travel fees or consultancies with CPAP and home-ventilation companies (ResMed, Elivie, Sefam, Philips Respironics, Nomics and others).

body: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin (DGSM), with DGPPN, DGN, DEGAM and others (AWMF S3)
guidelineTitle: S3-Leitlinie Insomnie bei Erwachsenen (AWMF 063-003), Version 2.0
recommendation: Secondary source: benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine receptor agonists 'in der Regel maximal vier Wochen' (as a rule a maximum of four weeks); 'Eine längere Anwendung wird aufgrund der Nebenwirkungen und der möglichen Abhängigkeitsentwicklung nicht empfohlen' (longer use is not recommended because of side effects and possible dependence).

body: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin (DGSM), with DGPPN, DGN, DEGAM and others (AWMF S3)
guidelineTitle: S3-Leitlinie Insomnie bei Erwachsenen (AWMF 063-003), Version 2.0
recommendation: Secondary source: 'Mittel der Wahl ist gemäß dieser jedoch ein nichtmedikamentöser Ansatz' (the treatment of choice is a non-drug approach, i.e. KVT-I / CBT-I).
conflictsOfInterest: Guideline has a COI table (Tab. 20) with AWMF management; not read.

body: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin (DGSM), with DGPPN, DGN, DEGAM and others (AWMF S3)
guidelineTitle: S3-Leitlinie Insomnie bei Erwachsenen (AWMF 063-003), Version 2.0
recommendation: Secondary source: sedating antidepressants (doxepin, trazodone) 'nur für die Kurzzeitbehandlung' (only for short-term treatment); a lexicon source quotes the guideline that without matching comorbidity they are not first choice.

body: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin (DGSM), with DGPPN, DGN, DEGAM and others (AWMF S3)
guidelineTitle: S3-Leitlinie Insomnie bei Erwachsenen (AWMF 063-003), Version 2.0
recommendation: Secondary source: PR melatonin is licensed 'für die Kurzzeitbehandlung bei von Insomnie Betroffenen ab 55 Jahren'; effects 'klein bis mittel'; no recommendation for long-term use; guideline advises buying melatonin products in pharmacies ('Beschaffung von melatoninhaltigen Präparaten in Apotheken') for product safety.

body: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin (DGSM), with DGPPN, DGN, DEGAM and others (AWMF S3)
guidelineTitle: S3-Leitlinie Insomnie bei Erwachsenen (AWMF 063-003), Version 2.0
recommendation: Secondary source: for orexin receptor antagonists 'keine Empfehlung für die Langzeitbehandlung ausgesprochen werden kann' (no recommendation for long-term treatment can be made); authors see 'klinisches Potenzial' for sedating antidepressants and orexin antagonists.

body: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin (DGSM), with DGPPN, DGN, DEGAM and others (AWMF S3)
guidelineTitle: S3-Leitlinie Insomnie bei Erwachsenen (AWMF 063-003), Version 2.0
recommendation: Secondary source: antihistamines get 'keine Empfehlung' despite being licensed; efficacy 'allenfalls geringgradig' with fast tolerance. Antipsychotics (melperone, pipamperone) 'werden in der Leitlinie trotz entsprechender Zulassung nicht empfohlen'. Phytotherapeutics graded 'sollte nicht' (should not). Exercise, light and art therapies get a 'kann' (may) recommendation.
strength: not verified (secondary source); phytotherapy 'sollte nicht'; light 'kann'

guidelineTitle: DiGA-Verzeichnis: digital health applications for insomnia
recommendation: Three insomnia DiGA are 'Dauerhaft aufgenommen' (permanently listed) for ICD-10 F51.0 (nichtorganische Insomnie) and G47.0 (Ein- und Durchschlafstörungen): HelloBetter Schlafen (GET.ON Institut; Herstellerpreis 241,25 €; no extra physician services required); somnio (mementor DE; 224,99 €; 'Vertragsärztliche Leistungen erforderlich'); somnovia (GAIA AG; 236,00 €; web only). All: 'Keine Mehrkosten' (no patient co-payment).
strength: Statutory reimbursement on prescription (§ 33a SGB V)

guidelineTitle: Arzneimittel-Richtlinie Anlage III Nr. 32 (hypnotics/sedatives prescribing restriction), amended 17 Aug 2023 for daridorexant
recommendation: Statutory health insurance excludes hypnotics/sedatives for sleep disorders, 'ausgenommen - zur Kurzzeittherapie bis zu 4 Wochen oder - für eine länger als 4 Wochen dauernde Behandlung in medizinisch begründeten Einzelfällen. Eine längerfristige Anwendung ... ist besonders zu begründen.' Separate exception: 'Daridorexant für die Behandlung von Schlafstörungen (Insomnie), deren Symptome seit mindestens 3 Monaten anhalten und eine beträchtliche Auswirkung auf die Tagesaktivität haben. Die Zweckmäßigkeit einer Weiterbehandlung ist innerhalb der ersten 3 Monate und anschließend in regelmäßigen Abständen zu beurteilen.'

guidelineTitle: S3-Leitlinie Schlafbezogene Atmungsstörungen bei Erwachsenen - Teil-Aktualisierung 2020
status: under revision (main guideline v3.1 Stand 23.12.2016, valid to 22.12.2021, 'in Überarbeitung'; 2020 partial update; 2023 amendment on residual daytime sleepiness)
recommendation: 'Polygrafiesysteme sollen bei hoher Prätestwahrscheinlichkeit zur Diagnose einer OSA eingesetzt werden (Evidenzlevel 2a, Empfehlungsgrad A)'. Polygraphy should not be used alone to diagnose or exclude OSA with lower pretest probability or suspected comorbid sleep disorders (EL 5, A). Polygraphy 'soll von schlafmedizinisch qualifizierten Ärzten durchgeführt werden' (A). Automatic scoring alone 'derzeit nicht zu empfehlen' (A). To exclude sleep-disordered breathing 'soll die kardiorespiratorische Polysomnografie durchgeführt werden; die Polygrafie ist nicht ausreichend' (A). Peripheral arterial tonometry 'sollte analog zur Polygrafie bei hoher Prätestwahrscheinlichkeit' be used (2a, B).
strength: Empfehlungsgrad A (soll) / B (sollte); Oxford evidence levels
conflictsOfInterest: AWMF COI process: disclosures rated low/moderate/high; moderate COI = excluded from voting on that topic, high = also from discussion (as described in the paper).

guidelineTitle: S3-Leitlinie Schlafbezogene Atmungsstörungen bei Erwachsenen - Teil-Aktualisierung 2020
recommendation: 'Neurostimulationsverfahren des N. hypoglossus sollten bei Patienten mit CPAP-Unverträglichkeit bzw. -ineffektivität mit einem AHI 15–65/h und einem BMI bis 35 kg/m2 sowie bei fehlenden anatomischen Auffälligkeiten und mittel- bis schwergradiger OSA erwogen werden (Evidenzlevel 1b, Empfehlungsgrad B)'. Also: positional therapy for mild-moderate positional OSA (1b, B); bimaxillary advancement 'soll ... erwogen werden' with small jaw when CPAP/oral appliance not possible (1b, A); tonsillectomy with UPPP for tonsillar hyperplasia (1a, A); nasal surgery when nasal obstruction causes CPAP intolerance (4, B).
conflictsOfInterest: AWMF COI process: disclosures rated low/moderate/high; moderate COI = excluded from voting on that topic, high = also from discussion (as described in the paper).

guidelineTitle: MVV-RL Anlage I Nr. 3: Polygraphie und Polysomnographie bei schlafbezogenen Atmungsstörungen
recommendation: 'Stufendiagnostik' (stepwise diagnosis): Stage 1 history incl. sleepiness questionnaires (e.g. Epworth); Stage 2 clinical exam; Stage 3 cardiorespiratory polygraphy 'während einer mindestens 6-stündigen Schlafphase', raw data 'stets visuell' reviewed by a qualified physician; Stage 4 PSG 'nur dann als ergänzende Diagnostik ..., wenn ... keine Entscheidung möglich ist, ob eine Therapie mittels CPAP ... notwendig ist', ideally two consecutive nights. Performing and billing PG/PSG requires KV approval (Genehmigung) under the § 135(2) quality agreement.

guidelineTitle: MVV-RL Anlage I Nr. 3 §4-5 (CPAP initiation and follow-up)
recommendation: §4: CPAP initiation 'soll ... unter kontinuierlicher polysomnographischer Überwachung in der Regel in zwei aufeinanderfolgenden Nächten durchgeführt werden' by the qualified physician, with Stage 1-3 results documented. §5: first control 6 months after start by polygraphy, checking device use ('Betriebsstundenzähler'); no further routine polygraphic controls if uncomplicated.

guidelineTitle: MVV-RL Anlage I Nr. 36: Unterkieferprotrusionsschiene bei obstruktiver Schlafapnoe
recommendation: Covered for adults with OSA confirmed by the stepwise diagnosis 'und eine Überdrucktherapie nicht erfolgreich durchgeführt werden kann' (and positive-pressure therapy cannot be carried out successfully). Only sleep-approved physicians may treat; device made and fitted by a contract dentist; protrusion set by dentist with physician, who checks effect.

guidelineTitle: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Sleep Disorders
status: stale (2017; IPS 2025 guideline cycle did not cover sleep)
recommendation: 'For the short term insomnia, pharmacotherapy is indicated, while for the chronic insomnia, cognitive behavior therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is preferred.' Drugs are 'not routinely recommended for the management of chronic insomnia'. But 'considering the limited availability of trained CBT-I therapist, consensus was reached that in certain circumstances where CBT-I is not possible for any reason, pharmacotherapy may be instituted for long term', citing Z-drug data out to 6 months. A common approach is to start drugs alongside CBT-I and then taper to CBT-I alone.

guidelineTitle: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Sleep Disorders
recommendation: Melatonin 3 mg tablets are available in India and 'may be used to induce sleep, however, data do not support its efficacy as a hypnotic agent. It is rather used as a chronobiotic.' Ramelteon (8-24 mg/day) and agomelatine (25-50 mg/day) are available. Sedating antidepressants (tricyclics, trazodone, mirtazapine) are for comorbid psychiatric disorders or when BZ/BzRA side effects are not tolerated. Over-the-counter antihistamines have limited efficacy data.

body: Indian Initiative on Obstructive Sleep Apnea (INOSA), under the Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
guidelineTitle: Consensus & Evidence-based INOSA Guidelines 2014 (First edition)
status: stale (first edition 2014; no second edition found)
recommendation: CPAP is the 'gold standard' for moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI >15) and an option for milder OSA. Treatment is indicated for AHI (or RDI) ≥15/h, or AHI ≥5 but <15 with sleepiness, impaired thinking or mood, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease or past stroke (Evidence Quality A, Strong Recommendation).
whatWasRead: full text (Lung India reprint; original Indian J Med Res 2014;140:451-68, PMID 25366217)
conflictsOfInterest: 'Source of Support: Nil Conflict of Interest: None declared.'

guidelineTitle: Consensus & Evidence-based INOSA Guidelines 2014
recommendation: Home (portable) testing (type 3/4) can be a useful, cost-effective and quick way to diagnose, but must be done only after a full sleep evaluation and with a practitioner qualified to run sleep studies (Evidence Quality B, Recommended). AHI may be falsely low because sleep time is not measured. Type 2 unattended PSG is also recommended (B).

guidelineTitle: Consensus & Evidence-based INOSA Guidelines 2014
recommendation: Surgery is recommended for patients who failed or cannot tolerate PAP. Bariatric surgery is 'strongly recommended' for obese OSA patients with BMI ≥35 kg/m2 (Evidence Quality B), with a repeat PSG afterwards. Oral appliances, made by sleep-trained dentists, are for snoring or mild-to-moderate OSA. Modafinil and armodafinil are 'the only agents approved' for daytime sleepiness that remains despite adequate PAP (Evidence Quality A, Strong).

guidelineTitle: Management of Persistent, Post-adenotonsillectomy Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Children: An Official ATS Clinical Practice Guideline
recommendation: 'up to 40% of children may have persistent OSA' after adenotonsillectomy. Six conditional suggestions: CPAP if not suited to site-specific surgery; orthodontic or dentofacial treatment for specific craniofacial features; weight loss if obese; lingual tonsillectomy; supraglottoplasty for sleep-dependent laryngomalacia; 'children on intranasal steroids with persistent OSA may be treated with montelukast'.
strength: Conditional, very low certainty (all six; GRADE)
conflictsOfInterest: Funded by ATS. Almeida is on the Somnomed clinical advisory board; no other conflicts.

body: International Pediatric Sleep Association (IPSA) Melatonin Task Force
guidelineTitle: Melatonin use in typically developing (TD) children: IPSA Expert Consensus Recommendations for Healthcare Providers
recommendation: Consensus recommendations on 'appropriate indications for melatonin in children, considerations regarding timing and dosage, safety issues and caveats'. The specific recommendations are not given in the abstract.

guidelineTitle: Partial endorsement of the AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline
recommendation: Survey of 53 national sleep societies, of which 23 responded. Of 20 AASM recommendations: 12 fully supported, 5 partially supported, 2 (dopamine agonists) 'endorsed with caveats' and 1 (dipyridamole) not supported. 'the avoidance of dopaminergic agents generated regional disagreement.' Barriers included 'limited access to certain medications (e.g., IV iron, gabapentin enacarbil)'.
conflictsOfInterest: Ferri reports WSS board membership. Others declare none.

body: International RLS Study Group (IRLSSG), European RLS Study Group (EURLSSG), RLS Foundation
guidelineTitle: Guidelines for the first-line treatment of RLS/WED, prevention and treatment of dopaminergic augmentation
status: stale (last updated 2016); in practice superseded by AASM 2025 and the RLS Foundation 2026 algorithm
recommendation: 'α2δ ligands may be considered for initial RLS/WED treatment'. Alternatively, if dopaminergic drugs are chosen first, 'the daily dose should be as low as possible and not exceed that recommended'. Patients with low iron stores should get iron. For severe augmentation, switch to an α2δ ligand or rotigotine, or consider an opioid.
strength: Evidence- and consensus-based task force (no GRADE)

guidelineTitle: Evidence-based and consensus clinical practice guidelines for the iron treatment of RLS/WED in adults and children
recommendation: 'Ferric carboxymaltose (1000 mg) is effective for treating moderate to severe RLS in those with serum ferritin <300 μg/l and could be used as first-line treatment for RLS in adults. Oral iron (65 mg elemental iron) is possibly effective ... in those with serum ferritin ≤75 μg/l.' There was insufficient evidence for children.
strength: Class I evidence for IV iron (4 studies); consensus algorithms

guidelineTitle: Guidance on appropriate prescribing of benzodiazepines and z-drugs (BZRA) for the treatment of anxiety and insomnia
recommendation: 'The MMP recommends that BZRA should only be prescribed for a period of a few days to two weeks for the treatment of insomnia.' Cites DoH Good Practice Guidelines (2002): hypnotic benzodiazepine prescriptions 'limited to between 2 - 4 weeks'; 'Do not prescribe for longer than four weeks'. 'Zolpidem should only be prescribed for patients with sleep-onset insomnia'; 'Zopiclone is suitable for continuous sleep disturbance.' First line: 'The MMP recommends The Good Sleep Guide as a first-line treatment for insomnia in new patients.'

body: Italian Insomnia Expert Consensus Group (members of Italian sleep/psychiatry/neurology societies)
guidelineTitle: Evaluation and management of insomnia in the clinical practice in Italy: a 2023 update from the Insomnia Expert Consensus Group
recommendation: 'Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia should be the first option according to availability.' Z-drug or short-acting BZ (in <65 y) 'in the short term (≤ 4 weeks)'; 'eszopiclone ... may be used for up to 6 months, also in the elderly'; melatonin 2 mg PR in adults ≥55 'for up to 13 weeks'; daridorexant 'can be used for at least 3 months and up to 1 year'.

guidelineTitle: Italian adaptation of international recommendations for the management of restless legs syndrome
recommendation: 'α2δ ligands are preferred for most adults with chronic persistent RLS, whereas dopamine agonists should be restricted to selected patients and monitored for augmentation.' Refractory or augmented RLS should be managed by clinicians with RLS expertise. 'Dipyridamole is not included in the standard pathway.'
conflictsOfInterest: No financial interests declared. Authors are unpaid members of the RLS-Italia committee.

body: MHLW-funded research group on appropriate use and discontinuation of hypnotics + Japanese Society of Sleep Research (JSSR) working group
guidelineTitle: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Appropriate Use and Discontinuation of Hypnotics (睡眠薬の適正な使用と休薬のための診療ガイドライン)
status: stale (first ed. 25 June 2013, revised 22 Oct 2013; errata page references a 22 July 2014 version; no later edition found)
recommendation: Built around 40 clinical questions running from first treatment through sleep hygiene and CBT, insomnia with other conditions, chronic insomnia, setting a treatment end-point and methods for stopping hypnotics. Recommendations come from evidence where available and expert consensus otherwise, with a parallel set written for patients. The treatment algorithm names an explicit 'end of treatment' and asks doctor and patient to decide together (shared decision-making) whether to aim for tapering/stopping or for 'safe long-term maintenance'.
strength: Grades not seen (full text not read)
whatWasRead: abstract (Mishima 2015 summary article) + secondary source (web-search summaries of the JSSR PDF); the guideline PDF itself was blocked (connection refused)

guidelineTitle: Approval of suvorexant (Belsomra, MSD K.K.)
recommendation: MHLW approved suvorexant on 26 September 2014, and Japan launched it in November 2014, ahead of any other country. It was not the world's first approval: the US FDA approved it on 13 August 2014, and the US launch waited for DEA scheduling until February 2015.
whatWasRead: abstract (Yang 2014: 'approved in the US in August 2014'; Japan 'preregistration') + secondary source (Japanese trade press search snippets for the 26 Sept 2014 approval and November launch)

guidelineTitle: Approval of lemborexant (Dayvigo, Eisai)
recommendation: Eisai announced Japanese approval of lemborexant 2.5, 5 and 10 mg tablets for insomnia on 23 January 2020. It was added to the NHI drug price list on 22 April 2020. The US FDA had approved it in December 2019.
whatWasRead: secondary source (search-result summaries of the press release; page not opened)

guidelineTitle: Approval of daridorexant (Quviviq, Nxera Pharma Japan; co-developed with Mochida; sold by Shionogi)
recommendation: MHLW approval of daridorexant 25 mg and 50 mg 'for the treatment of adult patients with insomnia' was announced on 24 September 2024. Japanese trade press says it launched in December 2024.

body: MHLW national medical fee schedule (psychotropic polypharmacy and long-term prescribing reductions)
guidelineTitle: Medical fee revisions 2012, 2014, 2016, 2018 (and 2020) on hypnotic/anxiolytic prescribing
status: current (rules carried forward; further revision April 2020)
recommendation: Payments to the prescriber are cut for: 3 or more anxiolytics or 3 or more hypnotics in one prescription (2012); this extended in 2014 (to all doctors, not just psychiatrists, per a Japanese secondary source); 3 or more drugs across anxiolytics, hypnotics, antidepressants or antipsychotics (2016); and, from April 2018, prescribing the same benzodiazepine receptor agonist continuously for 12 months or more to patients with anxiety or insomnia.
whatWasRead: abstract (Hirano 2019) + abstract (Takeshima 2023, PMID 36579672, DOI 10.1111/pcn.13525, free in PMC11488605)
conflictsOfInterest: Hirano 2019: first author's address is pfizer.com (Pfizer employee). Takeshima 2023: not seen.

body: Japanese Respiratory Society + MHLW Refractory Respiratory Diseases research group, with Japanese Society of Sleep Research and others
guidelineTitle: Sleep Apnea Syndrome (SAS) Clinical Practice Guidelines 2020
status: current (Japanese version July 2020; listed by Minds July 2021; English version of therapy CQs 2022)
recommendation: 36 clinical questions; the English version gives the treatment and management CQs (CQ16-36). The abstract says health insurance began covering CPAP in 1998 and the number of CPAP users in Japan is 'about to exceed 500,000'. Specific CPAP, oral appliance and surgery wording was not read.
conflictsOfInterest: Many panel members declare industry ties: lecture fees, research funds or industry-donated university courses from CPAP makers and suppliers (Philips Japan, ResMed, Teijin, Fukuda Denshi, Fukuda Lifetech) and from hypnotic makers (Eisai, MSD, Takeda). About 16 of 33 authors declare no COI.

body: MHLW national medical fee schedule, C107-2 注3/注4
guidelineTitle: Remote-monitoring add-on and video/phone management for home CPAP
status: current (remote-monitoring add-on created in FY2018; online-management item present in FY2026 version)
recommendation: Clinics meeting the standard can bill a remote-monitoring add-on (150 points per month, up to 2 months, billed at the next in-person visit) when they track usage and AHI through a connected device between visits and give guidance by phone or video. A separate item (209 points, in place of the 240-point fee) covers management through information and communication devices, once symptom improvement has been confirmed face to face after CPAP starts.
whatWasRead: secondary source (annotated copy of official notice)

body: MHLW national medical fee schedule, C107-2 notes (4) and (6)
guidelineTitle: FY2026 fee schedule: home CPAP management fee, continuation and usage rules
recommendation: The management fee continues only for patients judged able to keep going after assessing up to the first 2 months of treatment. After the first 3 months at that clinic, the fee cannot be billed if average CPAP use was under 1 hour a day in every one of the previous 3 months (the device-supply add-on can still be billed). An FY2026 clarification says the fee can be billed if any one of the 3 months averaged ≥1 hour/day. The clinic lends the CPAP device to the patient.
whatWasRead: secondary source (annotated copy of official notice and Q&A)

body: MHLW national medical fee schedule (診療報酬), item C107-2 在宅持続陽圧呼吸療法指導管理料
guidelineTitle: FY2026 (令和8年度) fee schedule: home CPAP management fee 2, eligible patients
recommendation: CPAP is covered (fee 2, criterion ウ) when all three hold: (イ) AHI ≥15; (ロ) strong symptoms such as daytime sleepiness or morning headache that disrupt daily life; (ハ) polysomnography shows sleep fragmentation and loss of deep sleep that CPAP normalises. Patients with AHI ≥30 qualify on symptoms (ロ) alone. Before FY2026 the cut-offs were widely given as AHI ≥20 on in-lab PSG or AHI ≥40 on a home (simplified) test, with symptoms.
whatWasRead: secondary source: annotated copy of the official notice (page text read), plus a hospital patient leaflet (Juntendo Shizuoka) for the earlier AHI 40 home test / AHI 20 PSG rule

guidelineTitle: Melatonin regulatory status (Melatobel granules, Nobelpharma)
recommendation: In Japan melatonin is a prescription drug. The only approved product, Melatobel granules (2020), is for children: sleep-onset problems in children with neurodevelopmental disorders. No melatonin product is approved for adult insomnia. Adults get the melatonin receptor agonist ramelteon instead.
whatWasRead: secondary source (search summaries); trial abstract (phase III, ages 6-15, 1/2/4 mg)

body: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare / PMDA (Nobelpharma product Melatobel)
guidelineTitle: Melatobel (melatonin granules) approval
recommendation: Melatonin granules (Melatobel) are approved in Japan for sleep-onset difficulty in children with neurodevelopmental disorders. The pivotal study was a 26-week, uncontrolled, open-label phase III trial in 99 children aged 6-15, using 1, 2 or 4 mg. Sleep-onset latency shortened by a mean of 36.7 minutes.
whatWasRead: abstract (trial); approval facts from secondary source (search results); PMDA label not read
conflictsOfInterest: Trial funded by and co-authored with Nobelpharma employees.

body: Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (IMSS) / CENETEC clinical practice guideline
guidelineTitle: Guía de práctica clínica. Diagnóstico y tratamiento del insomnio en el adulto mayor
recommendation: For older adults: find and treat secondary causes, use non-drug therapy including sleep hygiene, then drugs. "No es recomendable comenzar el tratamiento con un hipnótico" before ruling out causative drugs/diseases. "Tampoco se recomienda el uso de neurolépticos, melatonina, antihistamínicos o benzodiacepinas de vida media larga" (antipsychotics, melatonin, antihistamines and long-acting benzodiazepines not recommended).

guidelineTitle: NHG-Standaard Slaapproblemen (M23)
status: current (first published July 2014; latest revision with literature search Sept 2022/Aug 2023; site shows 'Laatste aanpassing: oktober 2026')
recommendation: 'We bevelen gedragsmatige behandeling aan bij aanhoudende slapeloosheid, bestaande uit ontspanningsoefeningen, stimuluscontrole en/of slaaprestrictie.' Work group: 'sterke aanbeveling'. Choose 'een passende, zo licht mogelijke aanpak': social domain (self-help, group course) or primary care (GP practice, e.g. with POH-ggz mental-health nurse, or sleep exercise therapist); a psychologist can add cognitive therapy.
conflictsOfInterest: not stated on page read (methods PDF 'totstandkoming en methoden' not read)

guidelineTitle: NHG-Standaard Slaapproblemen (M23)
status: current (first published July 2014; latest revision with literature search Sept 2022/Aug 2023; site shows 'Laatste aanpassing: oktober 2026')
recommendation: 'We bevelen slaapmiddelen niet aan bij patiënten met slapeloosheid' (we do not recommend sleeping pills). 'Overweeg slaapmiddelen alleen bij patiënten met kortdurende slapeloosheid met duidelijke relatie met een oorzaak, bij hoge lijdensdruk. Schrijf in dat geval kortdurend, bij voorkeur eenmalig, voor.' Practical: agree duration 'zo kort mogelijk, bijvoorbeeld maximaal 2-3 weken'; only short-acting, e.g. temazepam 10-20 mg (elderly 10 mg) or zolpidem 10 mg (elderly 5 mg); 'maximaal 5-10 tabletten per keer', preferably intermittent (e.g. every 3rd night); no repeat prescriptions via the assistant.
conflictsOfInterest: not stated on page read (methods PDF 'totstandkoming en methoden' not read)

guidelineTitle: NHG-Standaard Slaapproblemen (M23)
status: current (first published July 2014; latest revision with literature search Sept 2022/Aug 2023; site shows 'Laatste aanpassing: oktober 2026')
recommendation: 'Probeer bij chronisch slaapmiddelengebruik de patiënt te laten stoppen via een minimale-interventiestrategie of via gereguleerde dosisreductie.' Minimal intervention = stop letter with or without evaluation visit; works best with ≤1 standard daily dose ('het lukt 30-50% van deze patiënten om op eigen kracht te stoppen'). Example stop letters are attached to the guideline.
conflictsOfInterest: not stated on page read (methods PDF 'totstandkoming en methoden' not read)

guidelineTitle: NHG-Standaard Slaapproblemen (M23)
status: current (first published July 2014; latest revision with literature search Sept 2022/Aug 2023; site shows 'Laatste aanpassing: oktober 2026')
recommendation: 'We bevelen het voorschrijven van antidepressiva, zoals amitriptyline en mirtazapine, voor slapeloosheid niet aan, vanwege onvoldoende bewijs voor de effectiviteit, en de (soms ernstige) bijwerkingen.' Antipsychotics: 'sterke aanbeveling tegen het offlabel voorschijven van quetiapine bij slapeloosheid' (very low quality evidence). Valerian: not recommended ('ontbrekende effect').
strength: Strong against (quetiapine); antidepressants not graded in extract
conflictsOfInterest: not stated on page read (methods PDF 'totstandkoming en methoden' not read)

guidelineTitle: NHG-Standaard Slaapproblemen (M23)
status: current (first published July 2014; latest revision with literature search Sept 2022/Aug 2023; site shows 'Laatste aanpassing: oktober 2026')
recommendation: 'We bevelen het voorschrijven van melatonine aan volwassenen met slapeloosheid niet aan, omdat dit geen klinisch relevant effect heeft.' Advice to patients: avoid 'melatonine zonder medische indicatie'.
conflictsOfInterest: not stated on page read (methods PDF 'totstandkoming en methoden' not read)

guidelineTitle: NHG-Standaard Slaapproblemen (M23)
status: current (first published July 2014; latest revision with literature search Sept 2022/Aug 2023; site shows 'Laatste aanpassing: oktober 2026')
recommendation: Psychologist: 'Verwijs bij aanhoudende klachten voor behandeling van slapeloosheid. Overweeg dit als initieel beleid bij ernstige langdurige klachten en/of bij matig ernstige psychische comorbiditeit.' Severe psychiatric comorbidity: refer for insomnia plus comorbidity. Occupational physician if work-related; Cesar/Mensendieck sleep exercise therapist as alternative to GP coaching.
conflictsOfInterest: not stated on page read (methods PDF 'totstandkoming en methoden' not read)

guidelineTitle: NHG-Standaard Slaapproblemen (M23)
recommendation: NHG background: 'Om het langdurig gebruik van slaapmiddelen te ontmoedigen stelde de overheid per januari 2009 voorwaarden aan de vergoeding van benzodiazepinen. Gebruikers moeten de benzodiazepines zelf betalen als ze niet aan specifieke voorwaarden voldoen.'

guidelineTitle: NHG-Standaard Slaapproblemen (M23)
status: current (first published July 2014; latest revision with literature search Sept 2022/Aug 2023; site shows 'Laatste aanpassing: oktober 2026')
recommendation: 'Verwijs patiënten bij een vermoeden van klinisch relevant OSA ... voor diagnostiek en behandeling naar long- of kno-arts of neuroloog, afhankelijk van regionale afspraken.' If behavioural sleep deprivation may explain symptoms, first test whether longer sleep helps. If OSA suspicion is weak and insomnia coexists, start behavioural insomnia treatment first and refer if OSA suspicion persists.
conflictsOfInterest: not stated on page read (methods PDF 'totstandkoming en methoden' not read)

guidelineTitle: Managing insomnia: Part 2 - pharmacological treatment
recommendation: "Non-pharmacological interventions are the preferred treatment for insomnia." Hypnotics "should be used for a maximum of four weeks (but often less)"; short-acting hypnotics "should be prescribed for no more than two to three weeks", ideally a few nights. Temazepam, triazolam and zopiclone are the medicines indicated for insomnia. No OTC products incl. sedating antihistamines recommended; limited evidence for quetiapine.

body: Medsafe / PHARMAC (via Medsafe MARC paper, March 2026)
guidelineTitle: Melatonin safety profile in adults (MARC meeting 12 March 2026)
recommendation: Since 10 Oct 2025, adults 18+ can buy from pharmacies (pharmacy-only) up to 30 days of melatonin for primary insomnia (immediate-release <= 3 mg or modified-release <= 2 mg) or 10 days for jet lag (IR <= 5 mg). Adults 55+ can still get up to 13 weeks after pharmacist consultation. Otherwise prescription. PHARMAC funds modified-release 2 mg (Vigisom brand) only for patients <= 18 years meeting Special Authority criteria; unsubsidised for adult insomnia.

guidelineTitle: Nasjonal veileder for vanedannende legemidler
status: current (first published 19 Oct 2021, last change 30 Apr 2025); replacement 'avhengighetsskapende legemidler' in consultation draft (March 2026)
recommendation: 'Behandlingsvarigheten med benzodiazepiner eller benzodiazepinlignende legemidler bør være så kort som mulig, maksimalt fire uker.' Indication: 'Søvnlidelser, vanligvis inntil to uker, maksimalt fire uker.' Intermittent use: benzodiazepines daily or every other day up to 14 days before a drug-free pause; Z-drugs every other evening. Up to 2 weeks can stop without taper; after 2-4 weeks taper gradually. Prescribe no more than the smallest pack.

guidelineTitle: Nasjonal veileder for vanedannende legemidler
recommendation: 'Fastlege skal ha hovedansvaret for å ordinere og rekvirere vanedannende legemidler til sine listepasienter utenfor institusjon'. Specialists, on transfer, 'bør ... kun ordinere og rekvirere det antall tabletter ... som er nødvendig frem til fornyet vurdering hos fastlege'. 'Før oppstart ... bør lege i samråd med pasient vurdere behandling med andre behandlingsmetoder'.

body: Saudi sleep medicine experts (e-Delphi; Saudi Sleep Medicine Group helped recruit)
guidelineTitle: Using benzodiazepines and Z-drugs for managing primary insomnia in adults in Saudi Arabia: an e-Delphi study to aid the development of clinical guidelines
status: pre-guideline consensus; no national guideline found
recommendation: Over three Delphi rounds (2018; 15, 17 and then 11 experts), 16 statements on benzodiazepine and Z-drug use reached ≥80% agreement for inclusion in future Saudi guidelines; 5 were rejected. The statement texts were not read.

body: Agency for Care Effectiveness (ACE), Ministry of Health
guidelineTitle: (none found)
recommendation: No ACE Clinical Guidance on insomnia or OSA was found; the ACE topics seen include GAD, gout, asthma and osteoporosis. SingHealth education pieces call CBT-I first-line and mention 'stringent regulations of hypnotic agents, such as benzodiazepines' in Singapore.
whatWasRead: secondary source (search summaries; ACE site not opened)

body: Korean Society of Sleep Medicine / Korean Neuropsychiatric Association authors (adapted guideline)
guidelineTitle: Korean Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Insomnia in Adults
status: current but nearing stale (adapted from guidelines from about 2015-2017; no update found)
recommendation: 'We recommend priority implementation of Cognitive Behavioral Treatment for insomnia (CBT-I) in adults.'
conflictsOfInterest: 'The authors have no potential conflicts of interest to disclose.'

guidelineTitle: Korean Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Insomnia in Adults
recommendation: Clinicians may consider zolpidem IR (sleep onset), zolpidem CR (onset and maintenance), eszopiclone and zaleplon (onset), triazolam (onset; moderate evidence), low-dose doxepin and trazodone (maintenance), and ramelteon (onset). Each is phrased 'We recommend that clinicians consider using…'. Suvorexant for maintenance is graded Strong (low evidence), even though the text says 'It is not yet utilized in Korea.'
strength: Weak / low evidence for each (triazolam: moderate evidence); suvorexant: Strong / low

body: Korean Food and Drug Administration (now MFDS), as reported in the guideline
guidelineTitle: Benzodiazepine approvals for insomnia (as described in Choi et al. 2020)
recommendation: 'The following benzodiazepines are approved by the Korean Food and Drug Administration (KFDA) for short-term insomnia treatment (up to 4 weeks): flurazepam, triazolam, flunitrazepam, and brotizolam.' Lorazepam, clonazepam, diazepam and etizolam are not approved for insomnia but are used off-label.

guidelineTitle: Korean Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Insomnia in Adults
recommendation: Do not use immediate-release melatonin for adult insomnia (weak). Consider prolonged-release melatonin for sleep-maintenance insomnia in people aged 55 or older (weak, low evidence). Do not use doxylamine (strong, low), diphenhydramine or valerian. Teach patients on benzodiazepines or BzRAs during CBT-I to take them at bedtime (weak).
strength: IR melatonin: Weak against; PR melatonin ≥55 y: Weak for; doxylamine: Strong against

body: Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS)
guidelineTitle: Approval of lemborexant (Dayvigo, Eisai Korea); daridorexant pending
recommendation: MFDS approved lemborexant on 23 June 2026 for 'adult patients aged 18 years and older who have difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep'. For daridorexant, Nxera Pharma Korea has filed for marketing authorisation and expects approval in 2027 (trade press, March 2026).

body: Korean Society of Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery + Korean Society of Sleep and Breathing
guidelineTitle: Clinical Practice Guideline: Clinical Efficacy of Nasal Surgery in the Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea
recommendation: Ten key action statements on nasal surgery (septoplasty, turbinate, nasal valve, septorhinoplasty, sinus surgery) for OSA, mainly to make PAP more comfortable and improve quality of life: 3 strong recommendations, 3 recommendations and 4 options (ACP grading).
conflictsOfInterest: 'No potential conflict of interest relevant to this article was reported.'

guidelineTitle: NHIS coverage of polysomnography and PAP for OSA (since 1 July 2018)
recommendation: Since July 2018, national insurance pays for PSG and CPAP rental for patients who meet OSA criteria (CPAP prescribed for AHI ≥15, or AHI ≥5 with OSA symptoms or conditions such as sleepiness, disturbed sleep, hypertension, heart disease or past stroke). To keep coverage after the trial period, the patient must use the device ≥4 h a night on ≥70% of 30 consecutive nights (21 days) within the first 3 months.
whatWasRead: full text of a clinical study describing the rule (secondary to the NHIS notice)

guidelineTitle: International Consensus Document on Obstructive Sleep Apnea
recommendation: Abstract only: consensus 'based on a critical analysis of the latest literature' by 56 specialists from 17 societies with a Cochrane Iberoamerican methodologist; main document plus online systematic-search manuscripts. Specific recommendations not read.

body: SBU (Swedish Agency for Health Technology Assessment)
guidelineTitle: Behandling av sömnbesvär hos vuxna (SBU report, 2010)
recommendation: 'Psykologiska behandlingsmetoder i form av kognitiv beteendeterapi (KBT) och annan beteendeterapi leder till att patienten somnar snabbare och inte är vaken lika länge under natten. Även sömnkvaliteten blir bättre. Om man vill satsa mer på psykologiska behandlingsmetoder förutsätts att fler terapeuter utbildas.'

body: SBU (Swedish Agency for Health Technology Assessment)
guidelineTitle: Behandling av sömnbesvär hos vuxna (SBU report, 2010)
recommendation: 'Kortvarig behandling med zolpidem, zopiklon och zaleplon ... medför jämfört med placebo att patienten somnar snabbare och får längre total sömntid. Sådan behandling innebär en viss risk för biverkningar.' Prescribers should first choose 'preparat som är dokumenterat effektiva'. Evidence 'otillräckligt' for valerian/herbal and other complementary methods.

body: Swiss Society for Sleep Research, Sleep Medicine and Chronobiology (SGSSC), SIG 'Mental Health'
guidelineTitle: Behandlungsempfehlungen für chronische Insomnie - kognitive Verhaltenstherapie als Erstlinienbehandlung
recommendation: Companion article to SGSSC treatment recommendations: CBT-I first line; 'Am wirksamsten ist die Bettzeitbegrenzung' (bedtime restriction is most effective); CBT-I effective 'auch in verkürzten Formaten, digital oder von anderen Berufsgruppen durchgeführt'; 'Die Zahl der Therapieplätze ist noch immer unzureichend.'

guidelineTitle: Restriction on Z-drugs after complex sleep behaviours
recommendation: TFDA 'banned doctors from prescribing medicine containing any of four ingredients' (eszopiclone, zaleplon, zolpidem, zopiclone) to patients who have had sleepwalking or similar movements while partly conscious. Three of the four were already Class IV controlled drugs.

guidelineTitle: British Association for Psychopharmacology consensus statement on evidence-based treatment of insomnia, parasomnias and circadian rhythm disorders: An update
status: stale (consensus meeting Oct 2017, published 2019; no newer BAP sleep update found on PubMed as of Oct 2026)
recommendation: 'CBT-based treatment packages for chronic insomnia including sleep restriction and stimulus control are effective and therefore should be offered to patients as a first-line treatment (A).' 'Both face to face CBTi and dCBTi are efficacious (A).'
conflictsOfInterest: Paper states: 'The author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest' and 'received no financial support'. Note: co-author Colin Espie is listed with a Big Health Ltd (Sleepio maker) affiliation in a 2021 PubMed record (PMID 34246110); the BAP paper itself declares none. Treat as a COI to verify.

guidelineTitle: Sleepio to treat insomnia and insomnia symptoms (MTG70, now HTG624)
status: current (published 20 May 2022; migrated to HTG624, 'recommendations... remain unchanged')
recommendation: 'Sleepio is recommended as a cost saving option for treating insomnia and insomnia symptoms in primary care for people who would otherwise be offered sleep hygiene or sleeping pills.' Medical assessment first for people at higher risk of other sleep disorders (e.g. pregnancy, comorbidities). More research needed vs face-to-face CBT-I: 'There is no direct evidence of its effectiveness compared with face-to-face CBT-I'.

guidelineTitle: Guidance on the use of zaleplon, zolpidem and zopiclone for the short-term management of insomnia (TA77)
status: stale (published 28 Apr 2004; last reviewed 31 Aug 2010, 'found nothing new'); still listed as current
recommendation: When, after due consideration of non-drug measures, hypnotic therapy is appropriate for 'severe insomnia interfering with normal daily life', hypnotics 'should be prescribed for short periods of time only, in strict accordance with their licensed indications'. Because of 'the lack of compelling evidence to distinguish between zolpidem, zopiclone or the shorter-acting benzodiazepine hypnotics', prescribe the one with the lowest purchase cost. Switch only for adverse effects of a specific agent; 'Patients who have not responded to 1 of these hypnotic drugs should not be prescribed any of the others.'

guidelineTitle: Temazepam 10mg/5ml Oral Solution SmPC
recommendation: 'Treatment should if possible be intermittent. The lowest dose which can control symptoms should be used. It should not be continued beyond 4 weeks.' Duration 'should not exceed 4 weeks for insomnia, including tapering off process.' Elderly: 'Half the normal dose... may be sufficient'.

guidelineTitle: Prescribed medicines review: summary
recommendation: In 2017-18, 1.4 million adults in England (3%) were dispensed benzodiazepines and 1.0 million (2%) Z-drugs. Continuously prescribed April 2015-March 2018: benzodiazepines 120,000; Z-drugs 100,000. 'Clinical guidelines specify that benzodiazepines should not usually be prescribed for longer than 2 to 4 weeks.' Benzodiazepine prescriptions keep falling; Z-drug rise 'started to reverse in 2014'.

guidelineTitle: Medicines associated with dependence or withdrawal symptoms: safe prescribing and withdrawal management for adults (NG215)
recommendation: Covers 'general principles for prescribing and managing withdrawal from opioids, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, Z-drugs and antidepressants in primary and secondary care.' (Detailed recommendations not extracted here.)

body: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA)
guidelineTitle: Improving information supplied with gabapentinoids (pregabalin/gabapentin), benzodiazepines and z-drugs (Drug Safety Update)
recommendation: All three classes 'are known to pose risks of addiction, dependency, withdrawal and tolerance'; product information and packaging get strengthened warnings. 'Prior to starting treatment with these medicines, a discussion should be held with patients to put in place a strategy for reducing or ending treatment.' Taper gradually: 'Tapering from a high dose may take weeks or months.' Points to NICE NG215.

guidelineTitle: British Association for Psychopharmacology consensus statement on evidence-based treatment of insomnia, parasomnias and circadian rhythm disorders: An update
recommendation: Long-term use: 'Use as clinically indicated (A).' 'In general, hypnotic discontinuation should be based on slowly tapering off medication (A).' 'CBTi during taper improves outcome (A).' Text: 'The available evidence does not suggest there is an unfavourable risk/benefit transition at 3–4 weeks for any agent.'
conflictsOfInterest: Paper states: 'The author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest' and 'received no financial support'. Note: co-author Colin Espie is listed with a Big Health Ltd (Sleepio maker) affiliation in a 2021 PubMed record (PMID 34246110); the BAP paper itself declares none. Treat as a COI to verify.

guidelineTitle: Zolpidem Tartrate 10mg Tablets SmPC
recommendation: Same 4-week cap as zopiclone ('should not exceed four weeks including the period of tapering off'). 'Elderly or debilitated patients may be especially sensitive... therefore a 5 mg dose is recommended.'

guidelineTitle: Zimovane 7.5mg film-coated tablets SmPC
recommendation: 'Treatment should be as short as possible and should not exceed four weeks including the period of tapering off. Extension beyond the maximum treatment period should not take place without re-evaluation of the patient's status, since the risk of abuse and dependence increases with the duration of treatment.' 'Elderly should be given a reduced dose.' New taper wording: schedule 'should be tailored to the individual'.

guidelineTitle: British Association for Psychopharmacology consensus statement on evidence-based treatment of insomnia, parasomnias and circadian rhythm disorders: An update
recommendation: Drug choice: 'efficacy, safety, and duration of action (A)'; also prior response and 'history of substance abuse or dependence (D)'. Shorter-acting drug (zolpidem or melatonin) for sleep-onset problems, slightly longer (zopiclone) for night waking. Antidepressants: 'Consider drugs for depression when there is co-existent mood disorder (A)'; 'Beware toxicity of TCAs in overdose'. Antipsychotics: 'no indication for use as first-line treatment (D)'. Low-dose doxepin 'is effective in insomnia (A)' but not available in Europe; non-selective antihistamines have 'a limited role (D)'.
conflictsOfInterest: Paper states: 'The author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest' and 'received no financial support'. Note: co-author Colin Espie is listed with a Big Health Ltd (Sleepio maker) affiliation in a 2021 PubMed record (PMID 34246110); the BAP paper itself declares none. Treat as a COI to verify.

guidelineTitle: Insomnia (CKS topic)
recommendation: NOT READ. cks.nice.org.uk returns 'CKS is only available in the UK' (HTTP 403) from this location. CKS is the main NICE primary-care source for insomnia drug choice, duration limits and melatonin-over-55 wording. A secondary summary (iatrox.com, not used as evidence) suggests CKS offers CBT-I first and limits Z-drugs to short courses; lead must open the page from a UK IP.

guidelineTitle: British Association for Psychopharmacology consensus statement on evidence-based treatment of insomnia, parasomnias and circadian rhythm disorders: An update
recommendation: Older adults: 'CBTi is effective and should be offered as a first line treatment where available (A).' 'When a hypnotic is indicated in patients over 55 years prolonged release melatonin should be tried first (B).' 'If a GABA-A hypnotic is used then a shorter half-life will minimise unwanted hangover effects (A).'
conflictsOfInterest: Paper states: 'The author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest' and 'received no financial support'. Note: co-author Colin Espie is listed with a Big Health Ltd (Sleepio maker) affiliation in a 2021 PubMed record (PMID 34246110); the BAP paper itself declares none. Treat as a COI to verify.

guidelineTitle: Daridorexant for treating long-term insomnia (TA922)
recommendation: 'Daridorexant is recommended for treating insomnia in adults with symptoms lasting for 3 nights or more per week for at least 3 months, and whose daytime functioning is considerably affected, only if: cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBTi) has been tried but not worked, or CBTi is not available or is unsuitable.' 'The length of treatment should be as short as possible. Treatment with daridorexant should be assessed within 3 months of starting and should be stopped in people whose long-term insomnia has not responded adequately.'

guidelineTitle: Circadin 2mg prolonged-release tablets SmPC
recommendation: Legal category: 'Prescription only medicine'. Indicated 'as monotherapy for the short-term treatment of primary insomnia characterised by poor quality of sleep in patients who are aged 55 or over.' Dose '2 mg once daily, 1-2 hours before bedtime and after food. This dosage may be continued for up to thirteen weeks.'

body: NHS England / NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT)
guidelineTitle: Adjunctive Sleepio in an IAPT service (service evaluation)
status: evidence of local practice, not national policy
recommendation: One NHS talking therapies service (Oxford Health) offered Sleepio to all patients endorsing a 'poor sleep' item at assessment for 12 months, in addition to routine care. National NHS Talking Therapies manual's position on insomnia was NOT read (england.nhs.uk bot-blocked).
conflictsOfInterest: Stott, Miller and Espie list Big Health Ltd affiliations (PubMed record).

guidelineTitle: Insomnia
recommendation: See a GP if changing sleep habits has not helped, 'you've had trouble sleeping for months', or it affects daily life. GP may offer CBT 'face-to-face with a therapist, or through an online self-help programme'. May refer to a sleep clinic if symptoms of another sleep disorder such as sleep apnoea. 'GPs now rarely prescribe sleeping pills'; they are 'only prescribed for a few days, or weeks at the most' if insomnia is very bad or other treatments have not worked. Over-the-counter sleep aids 'may help you sleep better for 1 to 2 weeks. They should not be taken for any longer.'

guidelineTitle: Insomnia (NHS inform)
recommendation: Self-help first (CBT-based self-help guide; 'You could try an online course like Sleepio' with a free NHS inform sign-up link). If habits don't help: 'your GP may refer you for... CBT-I'. Medication 'can be effective in the short term but it can also cause insomnia to get worse, cause addiction, or other side effects.'

guidelineTitle: Sleepio to treat insomnia and insomnia symptoms (MTG70, now HTG624)
recommendation: 'At a price of £45 per person, Sleepio is cost saving compared with usual treatment in primary care.' Based on 9 GP practices; costs lower at 1 year, 'mostly because of fewer GP appointments and sleeping pills prescribed'.
conflictsOfInterest: Underlying cost study (Sampson 2022) co-authored by Big Health staff (C Miller, Big Health Inc affiliation).

guidelineTitle: Daridorexant for treating long-term insomnia (TA922)
recommendation: Integrated care boards and NHS England must comply 'within 3 months of its date of publication'; Wales 'within 2 months' of final draft guidance. Committee: 'daridorexant is recommended for routine use in the NHS'. List price '£1.40 per day (£42 per pack of 30 tablets)'.

guidelineTitle: daridorexant (Quviviq) SMC2611
recommendation: 'daridorexant (Quviviq®) is accepted for restricted use within NHSScotland.' 'SMC restriction: in patients who have failed cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) or for whom CBT-I is unsuitable or unavailable.'

guidelineTitle: Solriamfetol for treating excessive daytime sleepiness caused by narcolepsy (TA758)
recommendation: 'Solriamfetol is recommended as an option for treating excessive daytime sleepiness in adults with narcolepsy with or without cataplexy. This is only if modafinil and either dexamfetamine or methylphenidate have not worked well enough or are not suitable.' Committee: usual order is modafinil, then dexamfetamine or methylphenidate; sodium oxybate and pitolisant availability 'varies in clinics across England'.

guidelineTitle: Clinical Commissioning Policy: Sodium oxybate (children) - patient pathway section
recommendation: 'Referrals to specialist sleep services can be made only from secondary care.' Narcolepsy: 'First line: Methylphenidate preparations ... Second line: Dexamphetamine, lisdexamphetamine, modafinil and atomoxetine'. Cataplexy: 'First line: Venlafaxine. Second line: Clomipramine and other SSRIs'. Sodium oxybate 'is classed as third-line treatment.'
strength: Clinical consensus (the policy says the line order 'varies across countries')

body: NHS England Specialised Commissioning (Clinical Reference Group for Paediatric Neurosciences)
guidelineTitle: Clinical Commissioning Policy: Sodium oxybate for symptom control of narcolepsy with cataplexy (children and adolescents aged 7 until 19 years)
recommendation: Funded only 'where attempts to control symptoms of narcolepsy with cataplexy have failed despite a trial of first and second line medications from each symptom group for at least three months'. Requires an ICSD-3 diagnosis, treated comorbid sleep disorders on polysomnogram, and MDT approval. Use is tracked (e.g. Blueteq). Stop if there is respiratory depression or an incomplete response at 3 months. After the 19th birthday, funding passes to local commissioners (CCGs/ICBs).

body: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
guidelineTitle: TA758: Solriamfetol for treating excessive daytime sleepiness caused by narcolepsy
recommendation: Solriamfetol is recommended as an option for adults with narcolepsy, with or without cataplexy, only if modafinil and either dexamfetamine or methylphenidate have not worked well enough or are not suitable. The committee noted that pitolisant and sodium oxybate are usually given third-line or later in the NHS, and that access is limited by individual funding requests.
strength: NICE TA (mandatory NHS funding within 90 days)
whatWasRead: guideline web page (read in Chrome by lead session, 2026-10-21)

guidelineTitle: Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome and obesity hypoventilation syndrome in over 16s (NG202)
recommendation: Moderate/severe: 1.6.1 'Offer fixed-level CPAP, in addition to lifestyle advice'. Mild with symptoms affecting quality of life/daytime activity: 1.5.2 offer fixed-level CPAP with lifestyle advice if any priority factor, or 'if lifestyle advice alone has been unsuccessful or is considered inappropriate'. Mild without symptoms: 'treatment is not usually needed'. Telemonitoring: 'Offer... for up to 12 months'. Auto-CPAP only in listed situations (e.g. intolerance, or same/lower cost). Heated humidification for dryness/rhinitis.

guidelineTitle: Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome and obesity hypoventilation syndrome in over 16s (NG202)
recommendation: 1.3.1 'Offer home respiratory polygraphy to people with suspected OSAHS.' 1.3.2 'If access to home respiratory polygraphy is limited, consider home oximetry' (may be inaccurate with heart failure or chronic lung disease). 1.3.3/1.3.5 Consider polygraphy or polysomnography if results are negative but symptoms are significant/continue. 1.1.3 Use Epworth; consider STOP-Bang; 1.1.4 do not use Epworth alone to decide referral.

guidelineTitle: Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome and obesity hypoventilation syndrome in over 16s (NG202)
recommendation: If unable to tolerate or declines CPAP (mild with symptoms, or moderate/severe): 'consider a customised or semi-customised mandibular advancement splint as an alternative to CPAP' if 'aged 18 and over' and 'optimal dental and periodontal health'. Semi-customised may be inappropriate with active periodontal disease, few/no teeth, or generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Follow-up at 3 months.

guidelineTitle: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnoea (IPG598, now HTG455)
status: stale (published 22 Nov 2017; moved to HTG455, 'The guidance itself has not changed')
recommendation: Evidence 'is limited in quantity and quality. Therefore, this procedure should only be used with special arrangements for clinical governance, consent and audit or research.' Patient selection by clinicians 'with special expertise in the management of obstructive sleep apnoea'.

guidelineTitle: Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome and obesity hypoventilation syndrome in over 16s (NG202)
recommendation: 1.7.3 'Consider tonsillectomy for people with OSAHS who have large obstructive tonsils and a body mass index (BMI) of less than 35 kg/m2.' 1.7.4 'Consider referral for assessment for oropharyngeal surgery in people with severe OSAHS who have been unable to tolerate CPAP and a customised mandibular advancement splint despite medically supervised attempts.' Positional modifier: consider in mild/moderate positional OSAHS if other treatments unsuitable; 'unlikely to be effective in severe OSAHS'.

guidelineTitle: Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome and obesity hypoventilation syndrome in over 16s (NG202)
recommendation: 1.4.1 'Discuss appropriate lifestyle changes with all people with OSAHS. Provide support and information on losing weight, stopping smoking, reducing alcohol intake and improving sleep hygiene'. 1.9.11 'Consider stopping treatment if OSAHS may have resolved, for example, with significant weight loss' - re-check after at least 2 weeks off treatment.

guidelineTitle: Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome and obesity hypoventilation syndrome in over 16s (NG202)
recommendation: Referral letter should include assessment scores, how sleepiness affects the person, comorbidities, occupational risk, oxygen saturation/blood gases. 1.2.2 'prioritise people with suspected OSAHS for rapid assessment if': 'vocational driving job'; job where 'vigilance is critical for safety'; 'unstable cardiovascular disease' (e.g. poorly controlled arrhythmia, nocturnal angina, treatment-resistant hypertension); pregnant; 'preoperative assessment for major surgery'; non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.

guidelineTitle: Miscellaneous conditions: assessing fitness to drive - Excessive sleepiness including OSA
recommendation: Suspected OSA with excessive sleepiness: 'Must not drive. Driving may resume only after satisfactory symptom control. If symptom control cannot be achieved in 3 months DVLA must be notified.' Moderate (AHI 15-29) / severe (AHI 30+) with sleepiness: 'Must not drive and must notify DVLA'; relicensing needs control, improved sleepiness and 'treatment adherence'; review every 3 years (car) / annually (bus, lorry). Mild (AHI <15) with sleepiness: must not drive until controlled.

guidelineTitle: Continuous positive airway pressure for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome (TA139)
status: current but partly superseded (published 26 Mar 2008; last updated 20 Aug 2021 - mild-OSA rec replaced by NG202 1.5.2)
recommendation: CPAP 'is recommended as a treatment option for adults with moderate or severe symptomatic OSAHS' (as quoted in NG202). The mild-OSAHS recommendation 'has been updated and replaced by recommendation 1.5.2' of NG202.

guidelineTitle: Tirzepatide for managing overweight and obesity (TA1026)
status: current (published 23 Dec 2024; last updated 1 Sep 2025); NO OSA-specific tirzepatide appraisal found
recommendation: Tirzepatide recommended for obesity only with 'initial BMI of at least 35 kg/m2 and at least 1 weight-related comorbidity' (BMI threshold 2.5 lower for some ethnic groups). NHS England phased rollout lists obstructive sleep apnoea as one of 5 qualifying comorbidities: now = 4+ comorbidities and BMI >= 40; 'From around June 2026' 4+ and BMI 35-39.9; 'From around March 2027' 3 and BMI >= 40.

guidelineTitle: Pitolisant (TA776) and solriamfetol (TA777) for excessive daytime sleepiness caused by OSA
recommendation: TA776: 'Pitolisant hydrochloride is not recommended, within its marketing authorisation,' for residual sleepiness in OSA despite CPAP or CPAP intolerance. TA777: 'Solriamfetol is not recommended, within its marketing authorisation,' for residual sleepiness in OSA.

guidelineTitle: The handbook to the NHS Constitution for England
recommendation: Legal right to 'start your consultant-led treatment within a maximum of 18 weeks from referral for non-urgent conditions' (applies to consultant-led sleep services). Pledge: 'patients waiting for a diagnostic test should have been waiting less than 6 weeks from referral'. NHS talking therapies: '75%... within 6 weeks... 95%... within 18 weeks'.

recommendation: NOT READ (cks.nice.org.uk UK-only). No NICE clinical guideline or technology appraisal on RLS found; CKS is the only national English source. BAP 2019 covers RLS only in pregnancy: 'Good sleep hygiene and lifestyle (D)', 'Keep caffeine low as it can exacerbate RLS (D)'.

Initial 12 weeks covered if 'AHI or RDI greater than or equal to 15 events per hour, or AHI or RDI greater than or equal to 5 events and less than or equal to 14 events per hour with documented symptoms of excessive daytime sleepiness, impaired cognition, mood disorders or insomnia, or documented hypertension, ischemic heart disease, or history of stroke.' Diagnosis by attended PSG or unattended home test (Type II, III, or Type IV with at least 3 channels).

body: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Medicare
guidelineTitle: Medicare NCD 240.4.1 Sleep Testing for OSA
recommendation: Effective 3 Mar 2009, Medicare covers Type I attended in-lab PSG; Type II or III devices 'unattended in or out of a sleep lab facility'; Type IV devices 'measuring three or more channels, one of which is airflow'; and devices measuring three or more channels including actigraphy, oximetry and peripheral arterial tone, when the person has signs and symptoms of OSA. Tests must be ordered by the treating physician or qualified non-physician practitioner.
