guidelineTitle: Diagnosis and management of childhood obstructive sleep apnea syndrome
recommendation: 'All children/adolescents should be screened for snoring.' Polysomnography for snoring plus symptoms or signs. 'Adenotonsillectomy is recommended as the first-line treatment of patients with adenotonsillar hypertrophy.' CPAP if adenotonsillectomy is not done or OSA persists. Weight loss if overweight. 'Intranasal corticosteroids are an option' for mild OSA when surgery is contraindicated, or for mild post-operative OSA.

body: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation (AAO-HNSF)
guidelineTitle: Clinical Practice Guideline: Tonsillectomy in Children (Update)
recommendation: Refer for polysomnography before tonsillectomy if the child is '<2 years of age' or has 'obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial abnormalities, neuromuscular disorders, sickle cell disease, or mucopolysaccharidoses'. 'Clinicians should recommend tonsillectomy for children with obstructive sleep apnea documented by overnight polysomnography.' Overnight inpatient monitoring if '<3 years old or have severe obstructive sleep apnea (apnea-hypopnea index ≥10 obstructive events/hour, oxygen saturation nadir <80%, or both)'.

guidelineTitle: Practice parameters for behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children
recommendation: For ages 0 to 4 years 11 months: 'unmodified extinction, extinction with parental presence, and preventive parent education are all rated as individually effective therapies' (Standards). 'graduated extinction, bedtime fading/positive routines and scheduled awakenings' are effective with less certainty (Guidelines). Evidence was insufficient for standardized bedtime routines and positive reinforcement as single therapies.

guidelineTitle: Health Advisory: Melatonin Use in Children and Adolescents
recommendation: 'Parents should talk to a health care professional before giving melatonin or any supplement to children.' Melatonin is 'not under FDA oversight like other over-the-counter (OTC) or prescription medications', and its content 'can vary widely', most in 'chewable tablets'. 'Many sleep problems can be better managed with a change in schedules, habits, or behaviors'. Choose a USP Verified product.

body: RLS Foundation Scientific and Medical Advisory Board (published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings)
guidelineTitle: An Updated Algorithm for the Management of Restless Legs Syndrome
recommendation: A practical algorithm for primary care. It covers behavioral approaches for intermittent RLS, new indications for oral and IV iron, 'gabapentinoids as first-line pharmacologic therapy for chronic persistent RLS', 'the risks of dopamine agonists and the precautions needed if they are used', and 'the important role of low-dose opioids'. It also covers peroneal nerve stimulation and buprenorphine.
conflictsOfInterest: not stated in abstract; authors overlap heavily with the AASM 2025 panel

guidelineTitle: Treatment of restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movement disorder: an AASM clinical practice guideline
recommendation: Good practice statement: test serum iron studies, including ferritin and transferrin saturation, in all patients with clinically significant RLS, ideally in the morning. Consensus thresholds for adults: oral or IV iron if ferritin ≤ 75 ng/mL or transferrin saturation < 20%; IV iron only if ferritin is 75-100 ng/mL. Children: supplement if ferritin < 50 ng/mL. 'These iron supplementation guidelines are different than for the general population.'

body: World Health Organization, Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP)
guidelineTitle: mhGAP guideline (3rd edition, 2023) / mhGAP Evidence Resource Centre
recommendation: Absence finding: mhGAP covers 11 topics (child and adolescent disorders, depression, psychosis and bipolar, epilepsy, dementia, alcohol, self-harm and suicide, drug use, other emotional and bodily distress complaints, conditions related to stress, anxiety). There is no sleep or insomnia module and no OSA content.

body: WHO Expert Committee on the Selection and Use of Essential Medicines
guidelineTitle: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (23rd list 2023; 24th list Sept 2025)
recommendation: No hypnotic is listed for insomnia: no Z-drug, orexin antagonist, melatonin or ramelteon. In the mental health section diazepam is listed only for anxiety disorders; in 2023 benzodiazepines for anxiety were limited to diazepam and lorazepam for 'short-term emergency' treatment of acute severe anxiety. Midazolam is listed for procedural sedation and diazepam for palliative care.

guidelineTitle: ICD-11, Chapter 07 Sleep-wake disorders
recommendation: ICD-11 adds a separate Chapter 7 for sleep-wake disorders and drops ICD-10's split between organic and non-organic sleep disorders. It covers insomnia, hypersomnolence, sleep-related breathing, circadian, sleep-related movement disorders and parasomnias. Chronic insomnia is 7A00 (≥3 months) and short-term insomnia 7A01 (<3 months); obstructive sleep apnoea is 7A41.

guidelineTitle: Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age
recommendation: Infants: '14–17h (0–3 months of age) or 12–16h (4–11 months of age) of good quality sleep, including naps.' Ages 1-2: '11-14 hours of good quality sleep, including naps, with regular sleep and wake-up times.' Ages 3-4: '10–13h of good quality sleep, which may include a nap, with regular sleep and wake-up times.'
